query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small, well‐distributed volume fraction (≈0.25–0.5 wt %) of Y2O3 nanoparticles into a CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will enable the formation of an adaptive, nano‐structured friction interface that maintains both a low coefficient of friction and an ultralow wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy with a homogeneous FCC solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.25–0.5 wt % Y2O3 nanoparticles into the CoCrFeNi matrix via powder metallurgy or a comparable composite processing method to obtain a uniformly dispersed nanoparticle-reinforced microstructure.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in air across a broad temperature range (RT to 800 °C), at controlled loads and sliding speeds matching previous tribological evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: The dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as nucleation sites for nano-coupled grain structures and promote the in-situ formation of a dense, nanocrystalline oxide (glaze) layer on the worn surface.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the nanoparticles will reinforce the alloy by impeding dislocation motion and promoting stable shear localization, thereby reducing friction. At higher temperatures, the nanoparticle/matrix interfaces catalyze tribochemical reactions that lead to the rapid formation of a protective, lubricious glaze layer, which minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified CoCrFeNi, the nanoparticle-reinforced alloy is expected to demonstrate a consistently low friction coefficient and a 1–2 orders of magnitude lower wear rate throughout the entire temperature range.
generation.baseline: The starting CoCrFeNi alloy exhibits acceptable performance at lower temperatures but suffers from surface softening, adhesive wear, and oxidative degradation at high temperatures, leading to increases in friction and wear.
generation.boundary: Valid for sliding tests conducted in air, under similar normal loads and sliding velocities, and within the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nanoparticle loading and dispersion quality required to optimize the adaptive friction interface are not fully established. Additionally, potential issues such as nanoparticle agglomeration or interfacial incompatibility might affect the effectiveness of the glaze layer formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy and another set with 0.25–0.5 wt % Y2O3 nanoparticles uniformly dispersed. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests in air over a temperature range from RT to 800 °C under the same load and sliding speed conditions.
measurements: Record real-time coefficient of friction using in-situ tribometry.
Measure wear rates by calculating wear volume per unit load and sliding distance.
Examine worn surfaces via SEM and XRD to detect the formation of a nanocrystalline glaze layer.
Assess nanoparticle dispersion via TEM or high-resolution SEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y2O3-reinforced CoCrFeNi samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the baseline alloy, or if no distinctive glaze layer is observed on the worn surface at high temperatures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

AbstractA novel metal matrix composite CrMnFeCoNi with Y2O3 as reinforcement phase was designed and manufactured by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering. After sintering at 900 °C for 5 min, the microstructure consisted of a FCC matrix and Y2O3 nanoparticles. The addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 increased the room temperature tensile strength of the CrMnFeCoNi base from 868 MPa to 1001 MPa, while the mechanical properties of the addition of 0.5 wt % Y2O3 composite decreased. In the meantime, the addition of Y2O3 had no significant influence on the coefficient of friction, while the addition of 0.25 wt % Y2O3 composite shows excellent wear-resistance.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, metal-matrix composites, Y2O3 nanoparticles, mechanical properties, tribological properties
